pradeep|Chemistry|0|9|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Bromine with caustic potash is the **Hofmann bromamide degradation**, and its defining
feature is that the amine formed has **one carbon less** than the amide:
R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4KOH ⟶ **R–NH₂** + K₂CO₃ + 2KBr + 2H₂O
**Step 1 — count the carbons needed.** Ethylamine is C₂H₅NH₂, with **two** carbons. The amide
must therefore have **three**.
**Step 2 — find the three-carbon primary amide.**
**(b) Propanamide**, CH₃CH₂CONH₂ ✓ — three carbons, and a **primary** amide with two hydrogens
on nitrogen, which the reaction requires. It gives CH₃CH₂NH₂, ethylamine ✓
The others:
**(a) Acetamide**, CH₃CONH₂ — two carbons, so it would give **methylamine** ✗
**(c) Formamide**, HCONH₂ — one carbon, giving ammonia ✗
**(d) Methyl cyanide**, CH₃CN — not an amide at all. It is a nitrile, and **reducing** it (not
Hofmann) would give ethylamine, with the carbon count preserved rather than reduced ✗
Option (d) is the instructive distractor: it does lead to ethylamine, but by a different
reaction. The question specifies bromine and caustic potash, which only an amide answers.
The loss of a carbon is the signature of this degradation, and it is the one thing to check
first in any Hofmann question.
∴ propanamide.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Nitration is an **electrophilic aromatic substitution**, and the electrophile is the
**nitronium ion, NO₂⁺** ✓.
The mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids is called the **nitrating mixture**,
and the sulphuric acid is there to generate the electrophile. It is the **stronger** acid, so
it protonates the nitric acid, which then loses water:
HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ ⟶ H₂NO₃⁺ + HSO₄⁻
H₂NO₃⁺ ⟶ **NO₂⁺** + H₂O
The nitronium ion then attacks the π cloud of the benzene ring, forming the arenium ion
intermediate, and loss of a proton restores aromaticity and gives nitrobenzene.
Note that nitric acid here behaves as a **base**, accepting a proton from sulphuric acid —
which is unusual enough to be worth remembering.
Why the others are wrong:
**(a) NO₂** is a neutral radical, not an electrophile.
**(d) NO₂⁻**, the nitrite ion, is **negatively** charged and so cannot attack an
electron-rich ring.
**(b) NO⁺**, the nitrosonium ion, comes from **nitrous** acid, and it is the electrophile in
**nitrosation** and in diazotisation — a different reaction.
The existence of NO₂⁺ is not merely inferred: it can be isolated in salts such as
NO₂⁺ClO₄⁻, and seen in the Raman spectrum of the nitrating mixture.
∴ NO₂⁺.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|18|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Basicity depends on how **available** the nitrogen lone pair is for donation. Anything that
delocalises it away from nitrogen weakens the base.
**(a) Benzylamine**, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ ✓ **most basic.** The ring is separated from the nitrogen by a
**–CH₂– group**, which insulates the two. The lone pair cannot reach the ring, so it stays
fully on nitrogen and is freely available. Benzylamine behaves as an ordinary **aliphatic**
amine, pKb 4·7.
**(b) Aniline**, C₆H₅NH₂ — the nitrogen is attached **directly** to the ring, so its lone pair
is **delocalised into the π system** over the ortho and para positions. It is much less
available, and aniline is a far weaker base, pKb 9·4.
**(c) Acetanilide**, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ — worse still. The lone pair is now pulled in **two**
directions, into the ring **and** into the carbonyl group. Amides are essentially neutral.
**(d) p-Nitroaniline** — weakest of all. On top of the ring delocalisation, the **–NO₂** group
at the para position withdraws electrons strongly by resonance, draining the lone pair
further. pKb about 13.
So the order is **benzylamine > aniline > acetanilide ≈ p-nitroaniline**.
The single structural idea that settles it: a **CH₂ spacer** between the ring and the
nitrogen restores full basicity, because resonance cannot cross a saturated carbon.
∴ benzylamine.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|22|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two comparisons decide the order.
**Anions are far stronger bases than neutral molecules.** NH₂⁻ and OH⁻ each carry a full
negative charge and an exposed lone pair; NH₃ and H₂O must donate from a neutral atom. So
both anions outrank both molecules.
**Within each pair, the less electronegative atom is the stronger base.** Nitrogen (3·0) is
less electronegative than oxygen (3·5), so it holds its lone pair **more loosely** and gives
it up more readily. Hence
NH₂⁻ **>** OH⁻  and  NH₃ **>** H₂O
Putting the two rules together:
**NH₂⁻ > OH⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O** ✓ — option (a)
The same conclusion follows from the strengths of the conjugate acids, since the weaker the
acid the stronger its conjugate base:
NH₃ (pKa 38) is a far weaker acid than H₂O (pKa 15·7), so **NH₂⁻ is a far stronger base than
OH⁻**
H₂O (pKa 15·7) is a weaker acid than NH₄⁺ (pKa 9·2), so **NH₃ is a stronger base than H₂O**
The practical consequence is familiar: **sodamide, NaNH₂, is a far more powerful base than
sodium hydroxide**, strong enough to deprotonate a terminal alkyne, which hydroxide cannot do.
∴ NH₂⁻ > OH⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|39|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Benzenediazonium salts lose N₂ very readily, and what replaces it depends on the reagent.
With **methanol** the alcohol acts as a **nucleophile**, and its oxygen takes the place of the
diazonium group:
C₆H₅N₂⁺HSO₄⁻ + CH₃OH ⟶ **C₆H₅OCH₃** + N₂ + H₂SO₄
The product is **anisole**, methoxybenzene ✓ — option (d).
The contrast with **ethanol** is the point worth learning, and it is the next question in most
textbooks. Ethanol behaves as a **reducing agent** rather than a nucleophile: it donates a
hydride, is itself oxidised to acetaldehyde, and the diazonium group is replaced by **H**,
giving **benzene**.
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₂H₅OH ⟶ C₆H₆ + N₂ + CH₃CHO + HCl
So one alcohol substitutes and the other reduces, and only the number of carbons
distinguishes them.
The other options:
**(a) benzene** ✗ is the **ethanol** product, the intended trap
**(b) 'benzenol'** ✗ means phenol, which would require warming with **water**
**(c) benzyl alcohol** ✗ has an extra carbon that nothing in the reaction could supply
The general value of diazonium salts is exactly this versatility: the same intermediate
gives phenol with water, benzene with ethanol, anisole with methanol, and aryl halides,
cyanides and azo dyes with other reagents.
∴ anisole.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|44|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Follow the two steps.
**Step 1 — diazotisation.** Aniline with NaNO₂ and HCl at **273–278 K** (0–5 °C) gives the
diazonium salt:
C₆H₅NH₂ ⟶ **C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻**  (A)
The low temperature is essential; above about 10 °C the salt decomposes to phenol.
**Step 2 — benzene in alkali.** Treating a diazonium salt with an **aromatic hydrocarbon** in
the presence of NaOH is the **Gomberg–Bachmann reaction**. The diazonium salt loses N₂ to
give an aryl radical, which attacks the benzene ring, and the two rings are joined:
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₆ --NaOH--> **C₆H₅–C₆H₅** + N₂ + NaCl + H₂O
The product B is **biphenyl** ✓ — option (c).
Why not the others:
**(a) C₆H₅N₂Cl** ✗ is the intermediate A, not the final product.
**(b) C₆H₅OH** ✗ would be formed by warming the diazonium salt with **water**, not with
benzene.
**(d) C₆H₅N=NOH** ✗ is the diazohydroxide, formed transiently in alkali but not isolated as
the product here.
The key observation is that benzene has no activating group, so it cannot undergo **azo
coupling** (which needs a phenol or an amine). Instead the reaction takes the radical route,
and the nitrogen is lost altogether rather than retained in an –N=N– bridge.
∴ C₆H₅–C₆H₅.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|5|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
A diazonium salt is stable only if the positive charge on the –N₂⁺ group can be **spread
out**, and only an **aromatic** ring can do that.
**(d) C₆H₅–N₂⁺X⁻** ✓ **most stable.** The benzene ring is directly attached to the diazonium
group, so the positive charge is **delocalised by resonance** over the ring as well as over
the two nitrogens. Benzenediazonium chloride can be kept in solution at 0–5 °C and even
isolated as the solid tetrafluoroborate.
The others cannot do this:
**(b) CH₃–N₂⁺** and **(a) CH₃CH₂–N₂⁺** — **alkyl** diazonium ions, with no π system at all.
The charge is localised, and they decompose **instantly**, even at 0 °C, losing N₂ to give a
carbocation. This is why primary aliphatic amines give alcohols with nitrous acid rather
than isolable diazonium salts.
**(c) C₆H₅CH₂–N₂⁺** — a benzyl diazonium ion. The ring is present but is separated from the
diazonium group by a **–CH₂–**, which blocks resonance. It is no more stable than an alkyl
one, though the benzylic cation it decomposes to is stabilised.
So the whole question turns on whether the ring is attached **directly** to the nitrogen.
That stability is what makes aryl diazonium salts so useful: they survive long enough to be
converted to phenols, halides, cyanides and azo dyes.
∴ C₆H₅–N₂⁺X⁻.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|6|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The two alcohols behave **differently**, and that contrast is the whole question.
**With methanol — substitution.** The alcohol acts as a **nucleophile**; its oxygen replaces
the diazonium group:
C₆H₅N₂⁺X⁻ + CH₃OH ⟶ **C₆H₅OCH₃** (anisole) + N₂ + HX
**With ethanol — reduction.** The alcohol acts as a **reducing agent** instead. It transfers
a hydride to the ring carbon and is itself oxidised to acetaldehyde, so the diazonium group
is replaced by **H**:
C₆H₅N₂⁺X⁻ + C₂H₅OH ⟶ **C₆H₆** (benzene) + N₂ + CH₃CHO + HX
So in the order asked — CH₃OH first, then CH₃CH₂OH — the products are
**C₆H₅OCH₃ and C₆H₆** ✓ — option (c).
Option (a) has the two **the wrong way round**, which is the intended trap, and options (b)
and (d) invent an ethyl ether that neither reaction gives.
Why ethanol reduces and methanol substitutes comes down to which pathway is easier for each:
ethanol has an α-hydrogen on a secondary-like carbon that is given up readily to form a
stable aldehyde, while methanol's oxidation is less favourable and its small oxygen is the
better nucleophile.
The practical use of the ethanol reaction is to **remove** an amino group from a ring
altogether — introduce it to direct a substitution, then diazotise and reduce it away.
∴ C₆H₅OCH₃, C₆H₆.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Compare the carbon counts of the starting material and the product.
**2-Phenylpropanamide** is C₆H₅CH(CH₃)**CONH₂** — nine carbons, with the amide carbon among
them.
**1-Phenylethanamine** is C₆H₅CH(CH₃)**NH₂** — eight carbons.
So the conversion **loses one carbon** while the nitrogen is retained as an –NH₂ in its place.
That is the signature of the **Hofmann bromamide degradation**, whose reagent is
**Br₂ with aqueous NaOH** ✓ — option (b).
R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH ⟶ **R–NH₂** + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O
The mechanism explains the lost carbon: the amide nitrogen is brominated, the bromamide
anion rearranges with **migration of R from carbon to nitrogen**, giving an isocyanate, and
hydrolysis of that releases the amine and CO₂.
The other reagents are all **reducing agents**, and a reduction would **keep** all nine
carbons, giving the wrong product:
**(a) excess H₂/Pt**, **(c) NaBH₄/methanol** and **(d) LiAlH₄/ether** would each reduce the
amide to the **amine with the same number of carbons**, C₆H₅CH(CH₃)CH₂NH₂ — one carbon too
many.
So the carbon count alone identifies the reaction before any mechanism is considered, and
that is the quickest way to answer this kind of question.
∴ NaOH/Br₂.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Nitrous acid distinguishes the three classes of amine, and **primary aliphatic** amines give
the most dramatic result.
Methylamine is a **primary aliphatic** amine, so HNO₂ **diazotises** it — but the aliphatic
diazonium salt formed is **far too unstable to survive**, even at 0 °C. It loses nitrogen at
once, leaving a carbocation which picks up water:
CH₃NH₂ + HNO₂ ⟶ [CH₃N₂⁺] ⟶ CH₃⁺ + N₂ ⟶ **CH₃OH** + N₂ ✓
So the product is **methanol** — option (c) — with **brisk effervescence of nitrogen** gas,
which is the visible sign of the test.
The contrast with the **aromatic** case is the point. Benzenediazonium chloride is stabilised
by resonance with the ring and survives at 0–5 °C, which is why aryl diazonium salts can be
isolated and used, while alkyl ones cannot.
For completeness, the other two classes:
**Secondary** amines + HNO₂ ⟶ a yellow oily **N-nitrosamine**
**Tertiary** aliphatic amines ⟶ simply form a soluble nitrite salt
Why the other options are wrong: (a) CH₃–O–N=O is methyl nitrite, which is not what forms
here; (b) dimethyl ether and (d) acetaldehyde would each require a carbon skeleton the
reaction cannot build.
The quantitative release of N₂ is the basis of the **Van Slyke method** for estimating amino
groups.
∴ CH₃OH.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|17|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Fe and HCl** is the standard industrial reduction of a nitro group, and it takes the
reduction all the way:
Ar–NO₂ + 6[H] --Fe/HCl--> **Ar–NH₂** + 2H₂O
So the product is an **aromatic primary amine** ✓ — option (c). Nitrobenzene gives aniline,
and this is in fact how aniline is manufactured.
Iron is preferred over tin for the industrial process because the FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed
by water to regenerate HCl, so only a **catalytic** quantity of acid is needed — a real
economy on a large scale.
The key point is that the **medium decides the product**, and only the acidic medium gives
the amine:
**acidic** (Fe/HCl, Sn/HCl) ⟶ **aniline**
**neutral** (Zn/NH₄Cl) ⟶ phenylhydroxylamine, C₆H₅NHOH
**alkaline** (Zn/NaOH) ⟶ hydrazobenzene; LiAlH₄ ⟶ azobenzene
**electrolytic in strongly acidic** medium ⟶ p-aminophenol
The distractors correspond to no reduction at all:
**(a) an oxime** would need a carbonyl compound and hydroxylamine
**(b) an aromatic hydrocarbon** would require the whole nitrogen to be stripped off
**(d) an amide** would need an acyl group, which is not present
∴ aromatic primary amine.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two rules settle the order.
**An anion is a much stronger base than the corresponding neutral molecule**, because it
already carries a full negative charge and an exposed lone pair. So NH₂⁻ and OH⁻ both rank
above NH₃ and H₂O.
**Within each pair, the less electronegative atom is the stronger base.** Nitrogen (3·0) holds
its lone pair less tightly than oxygen (3·5) and so donates it more readily:
NH₂⁻ **>** OH⁻  and  NH₃ **>** H₂O
Combining them, the decreasing order is
**NH₂⁻ > OH⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O** ✓ — option (a)
The same result follows from the conjugate acids, since the weaker the acid the stronger its
conjugate base. NH₃ has pKa 38 against water's 15·7, so **NH₂⁻ is enormously more basic than
OH⁻** — by more than twenty powers of ten.
That is not an abstract figure. **Sodamide (NaNH₂)** is strong enough to remove a proton from
a terminal alkyne, pKa 25, which sodium hydroxide cannot touch; and NH₂⁻ cannot exist in
water at all, since it deprotonates the solvent instantly:
NH₂⁻ + H₂O ⟶ NH₃ + OH⁻
That last reaction is the **levelling effect** in action, and it is itself evidence of the
order.
∴ NH₂⁻ > OH⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|7|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The Hofmann bromamide degradation needs a **primary amide**, –CONH₂, with **two hydrogens on
nitrogen**. The mechanism explains why:
base removes **one** N–H proton, bromine attaches to the nitrogen, then base removes the
**second** N–H proton to give the bromamide anion, which rearranges.
With fewer than two N–H hydrogens the sequence cannot even start.
**(a) CH₃CONHCH₃** ✓ **will not react** — N-methylacetamide is a **secondary** amide. Its
nitrogen carries a methyl group and only **one** hydrogen, so the second deprotonation is
impossible ✗
The others are all primary amides and react normally:
**(b) CH₃CH₂CONH₂** — propanamide ⟶ ethylamine
**(c) CH₃CONH₂** — acetamide ⟶ methylamine
**(d) C₆H₅CONH₂** — benzamide ⟶ aniline
Notice that the aromatic one, benzamide, works perfectly well: the restriction is on the
**nitrogen substitution**, not on whether the R group is aliphatic or aromatic. That is the
contrast with the **Gabriel synthesis**, which is restricted the other way — it makes only
**aliphatic** primary amines, because its key step is an SN2 on an alkyl halide.
In every case the amine produced has **one carbon less** than the amide, which is the quick
way to check an answer.
∴ CH₃CONHCH₃.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|18|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The phrase **'in gaseous phase'** is the key, because it removes solvation from the picture
and leaves only the **inductive effect**.
In the gas phase each extra alkyl group pushes electron density towards the nitrogen (+I),
making the lone pair more available, with nothing to oppose it. So basicity rises steadily
with substitution:
**CH₃NH₂ (I) < (CH₃)₂NH (II) < (CH₃)₃N (III)**
Benzylamine, **C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ (IV)**, is the **weakest**: the phenyl group is electron-withdrawing
relative to an alkyl group (the sp² carbons pull electron density), so it reduces the
electron density on nitrogen rather than increasing it.
Putting them together in **increasing** order:
**IV < I < II < III** ✓ — option (d)
**Why the aqueous order is different**, and why the question specifies the phase: in water,
three effects compete — the inductive effect, **steric hindrance** around a crowded nitrogen,
and **solvation of the cation by hydrogen bonding**. A tertiary ammonium ion has only one
N–H to hydrogen-bond with, so it is poorly solvated, and the tertiary amine drops down the
order. The familiar aqueous result for methylamines is
(CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N
In the gas phase there is no solvent, so that complication disappears and the simple
inductive order is restored. Noticing which phase the question names is the whole skill here.
∴ IV < I < II < III.
